name: Transblepharoplasty brow lift

lead: A transblepharoplasty brow lift raises the eyebrows from inside the upper eyelid, using the same incision as an upper blepharoplasty. Lifting a low or drooping brow can open the eye area, reduce a tired or heavy look and improve the space between brow and lid.

Surgeons describe it as a way to address the eyelid and brow together with minimal facial incisions and shorter operating time. It is reserved for selected patients, often those who are already having eyelid surgery.

paras: Through the blepharoplasty incision, the surgeon releases or repositions tissue and secures the brow, and may weaken the muscles that pull it down such as the corrugator and procerus. It is done by a plastic or facial plastic surgeon, usually together with upper blepharoplasty.

As with any surgery there are risks of bleeding, infection, asymmetry, scarring and changes in sensation. Results vary and revision is possible. The choice among brow lift techniques depends on anatomy and surgeon judgment.

angle.text: The procedure raises brow position and can reduce the heavy-lidded look, giving a more open, alert upper face. It is chosen by people who want brow elevation without a forehead or scalp incision.

lead: A transblepharoplasty brow lift, also called an internal brow lift, repositions the eyebrow through the incision made for upper eyelid surgery rather than through the forehead or scalp. A 2008 article in Annals of Plastic Surgery described it as a technique that is easy to perform, minimizes facial incisions and operative time, and can reach results comparable to more extensive approaches.[1]

The upper eyelid and brow work together, and surgeons commonly manage them as one complex. Review literature notes that upper blepharoplasty aims to improve appearance while keeping natural shape and function.[2] Another review describes the role of the brow depressor muscles and of corrugator and procerus myotomy during this approach.[3]
Other brow-lift routes include endoscopic, coronal, pretrichial, temporal and direct techniques. A Wikipedia overview lists the internal approach among the options.[4]

paras: The technique uses the eyelid incision to access the brow region, so no separate forehead incision is needed.[1] Surgeons may also release brow depressor muscles to let the brow sit higher.[3]

The first documented medical discussion of a forehead lift was by the German surgeon Erich Lexer in 1910.[4] Smaller-incision and endoscopic approaches later became alternatives to long coronal incisions, with the transblepharoplasty approach described as an additional option.[1]

General brow-lift literature reports complications as uncommon when performed by trained surgeons, with bleeding and infection possible in any surgery; different techniques differ in the risks they most often carry.[4] Brow position is judged subjectively, and what counts as low varies by person.[5]

Published work consists of surgeon-reported techniques and case series rather than randomized trials. The 2008 paper reported an expanded role for transblepharoplasty brow suspension,[1] and a 2013 review presented preferred technique and patient results.[3]
